narrative:
The model estimated a 76% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt, and that estimate drove the denial of your law school application. This is not a verdict on your ability, but it means the model judged the risk too high based on your profile.

The strongest factor was your third-year class standing: you were in the first decile, while accepted students averaged near the sixth decile, and this signal pushed the prediction toward failure. Your LSAT score was the second most influential factor; at 25, compared with an accepted-student average of about 37, it also pushed toward failure. The third most important factor was your lower-middle family income bracket, which is uncommon among accepted students at about 8.8%; in this case, it worked in your favor and pushed toward passing, but it was not enough to outweigh the academic and test-score signals. Your gender and race were not used in the prediction.

To move forward, ask admissions whether there is an appeal or reconsideration process and what evidence they will accept. If you reapply, focus on raising your LSAT score and strengthening your academic record. Consider retaking the LSAT, taking additional relevant coursework, seeking pre-law advising, and applying to schools where your profile is a stronger match.
